question: What does a real RL project involve, and how do you spot, define, engineer (environment, state, policy, actions, exploration, reward) and refine one?
contributions: An RL project life cycle (problem definition, environment/MDP refinement, then two phases left to ch. 10) contrasted with CRISP-DM style data science
Indicators for spotting an RL problem: sequential, strategic, entity, environment, state, action, quantifiable success
Taxonomy of learning regimes: online, offline/batch, concurrent, reset-free
Engineering guidance for environments, simulation, state, policy, action spaces, exploration and reward

results.claim: Adding a simple gripper-height measurement to an image-based robotic state improved pick-up of unseen objects by 12% (Kalashnikov et al., QT-Opt).
results.metric: improvement in pick-up of unseen objects
results.setup: Robotic grasping with images as the state representation, plus a 'height of gripper' measurement; baseline without it not described in the chapter.
results.quote: improved the robot’s ability to pick up unseen objects by a whopping 12%
results.note: Chapter does not say 12% of what (percentage points or relative); the QT-Opt paper was not read.

results.claim: As of 2020 no convergence proofs exist for nonlinear function approximators, so deep RL is not guaranteed to converge; linear approximators are provably convergent.
results.setup: Continuous state spaces with function approximation.
results.quote: As of 2020, no convergence proofs exist for nonlinear approximators

results.claim: Clipping rewards to +/-1 (as DQN recommends) treats Pac-Man dots and fruit alike; normalizing instead makes the DQN agent hunt ghosts and fruit.
results.setup: DQN on Pac-Man; no numbers or citation given in the chapter.
results.note: Quote kept short because of a hyphenated line break; the full sentence is 'DQN recommends clipping rewards to +/–1, but in the game Pac-Man this treats both dots and fruit as having the same reward'.

results.claim: A discrete grid for ride-share routing in New York had cells about 2 miles in diameter, so vehicles could end up 2 miles from the customer even after optimisation.
results.source: Chaudhari, Byers, Terzi 2020, Learn to Earn (arXiv:2006.10904)
results.setup: Ride-share fleet positioning policy on a discretised map of New York City.
results.quote: the diameter of each cell in New York’s grid
results.note: Quote is a fragment of 'was about 2 miles'; the value sits on the next line of the source text.

limits: A practitioner's account: almost no experiments or numbers of its own; claims are opinion or quoted from cited work.
Dated by 2020: offline RL is described as an open research problem; no LLM or RLHF content.
The author concedes that implementations are domain specific and that he has 'presented what I think is reasonable'.
Real-life interaction section says it 'does not sufficiently express' the engineering effort.
practices: Start simple: simplify the problem to the MDP and add detail later (opening of chapter).
Keep development cycles as small as possible; the time between git commits is one proxy (opening).
Pick RL when the problem is sequential and strategic; ML is single-step and myopic (Problem Definition).
Treat the environment as a bounded context behind an interface, and do not make it too big or complex (Low-Level RL Indicators).
Quantify success in units the stakeholder understands, such as money (Low-Level RL Indicators).
Build the environment first, as a Gym-style interface, to learn the data and avoid the 'improvement shotgun' (Environment Engineering).
Prefer an existing simulation; build your own only if it is a competitive differentiator, and expose the same aspects that are observable in real life (Simulation).
Do not over-trust a simulation: policies can fail in real life that work perfectly in simulation (Simulation).
Engineer the state for the best representation and let the policy solve the task, rather than crafting solving features (State Engineering).
Limit state and action counts to reduce exploration space (Low-Level RL Indicators).
Linear approximators with polynomial, Fourier or radial bases keep convergence guarantees; discretise via binning, tile coding or hashing for Q-learning (Continuous states).
For softmax over actions use advantages rather than raw values, with an exponential softmax (Binary actions).
For continuous actions predict a distribution mean (and std), starting with high std for exploration (Continuous actions).
For massive action spaces use policy gradients, embeddings, or rank the top-k items rather than choosing combinations (Massive action spaces).
Before intrinsic motivation, try better algorithms, intermediary rewards, imitation or denser rewards (Exploration).
Reward should be fast, correlate with the true reward, de-noised, encode nonfunctional requirements, consider time, prevent plateaus, be smooth and simple (Reward engineering guidelines).
Normalize rewards; clip with care; transform rewards cautiously (Reward shaping).
Do not chase the last 20%: use the Pareto principle in the analysis-design-implementation-evaluation loop (Process).
Expect initial RL results to be worse than an existing ML solution in the short term (RL Problems Are Sequential).

terms.definition: the number of interactions with an environment required to learn an optimal policy
training a new policy on a stored batch of data, such as a replay buffer, with no further interaction with the environment
coordinated exploration of the same environment by teams of independent agents with the joint task of exploring the state-action space (author notes the term is overloaded)
also called state representation learning: techniques that aim to improve how the observations represent the state
designing a policy that best solves a problem given a set of constraints
with linear approximators predicting multiple outputs, keep distinct parameters per action and update only the chosen action's parameters
building a model of an environment from offline data so the agent can interact as if online
a pair of networks, one random and fixed, one trained to predict its embeddings; prediction error is a novelty bonus added to the reward
throwing a bunch of different ideas at the problem hoping one hits, instead of understanding the environment
